description: We are building an open-source geospatial analytics platform and burning activity calendar that bridges the 25-year satellite record between NASA’s legacy MODIS (Terra/Aqua) and modern VIIRS (Suomi-NPP/NOAA-20/21) sensors.
summary:
FireScope is an interactive web app for exploring satellite observations of fires. It brings together active-fire data from NASA FIRMS, including MODIS and VIIRS detections, and presents them on maps, calendars, and charts. Users can explore activity by date, sensor, country, or region, and compare long-term patterns with a harmonized index that accounts for differences between satellite sensors.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex Earth-observation data easier to understand and explore. By showing where and when detections occur and how activity changes over time—FireScope can help people investigate fire.
details:
FireScope is a web app for exploring satellite observations of active fires. It retrieves data from NASA FIRMS, including MODIS and VIIRS observations, and displays detections and trends through interactive maps, calendars, and charts. Users can filter by date, sensor, country, or region. When no live-data retrieval has been completed, the app asks its backend to fetch data; historical country archives can also be prepared on demand.

The project makes complex satellite data more accessible and helps users explore where and when fire activity has been detected. Its key creative feature is a harmonized index that compares each sensor with its own historical record, rather than treating differing sensor measurements as directly equivalent. We also distinguish missing or incomplete coverage from confirmed zero detections, so gaps in the data are not mistaken for an absence of fires.

We built the frontend with Next.js, React, and TypeScript, and the API backend with Python and Django, hosted on Render. Mapping uses Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles, and charts use Recharts. Our team considered data coverage, sensor differences, geographic boundaries, and retrieval delays. The intended impact is to support exploration, research, and public understanding—not emergency alerts or response decisions.
